 ORL Toothpaste and Mouthwash Recall Covers 51,762 Units, Including Kids' Products, After FDA Tests Found Hormones
 Published Nov 17, 2026 8:31 PM EST 
 By
 Joseph James 
 Editorial Illustration via AI 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 About 51,762 units of ORL Organic Oral Care toothpaste and mouthwash sold nationwide have been recalled after Food and Drug Administration testing found progesterone, estradiol, or DHEA in samples, Parade reported . The FDA classified the recall as Class II on Nov. 6.
 The products come from ORL Labs LLC of Scottsdale, Arizona, which attributed the problem to cross-contamination . Three of the six recalled products are marketed for children, including bubblegum-flavored toothpaste and mouthwash. No illnesses have been reported.
 For parents, the concern is simple. Hormones such as estradiol, a form of estrogen, and progesterone are used in birth control and menopause treatment. They do not belong in a product children use twice a day.
 Products and Lots to Check
 The recall, which began Oct. 12, covers six products. The 4-ounce toothpastes are Bubblegum Kids Natural Toothpaste , UPC 850006245505, 3,976 units; Cinnamint Toothpaste, UPC 850006245512, 7,202 units; and Fresh Mint Natural Toothpaste, UPC 850006245499, 19,247 units.
 The 16.9-ounce mouthwashes are Bubblegum Kids Mouthwash, UPC 850006245475, 3,116 units; Cinnamint Kids Mouthwash, UPC 850006245468, 6,140 units; and Fresh Mint Mouthwash, UPC 850006245451, 12,081 units.
 The recall includes 37 lot numbers, with expiration dates from September 2026 through August 2028. Lots of the kids' bubblegum toothpaste include 241029P4, 250414P4, 250520P4, 260406P4, and 260511P4. Families can compare their packaging with the full lot lists published with the recall notice.
 The FDA's recall reason states that the company "was notified by the FDA of sampling results" showing the hormones, TheHealthy reported . The agency has not released the hormone levels it found. Class II drug recalls typically appear in the FDA's weekly enforcement report rather than in a public announcement, which helps explain why many shoppers are only now hearing about a recall that began in October.
 As of Nov. 10, ORL's website said it was temporarily pausing all orders for site maintenance, MedShadow reported .
 An Earlier Warning From the FDA
 This is not the first hormone-related recall tied to the brand. In December 2025, Phoenix manufacturer Signature Formulations recalled one lot each of ORL kids' bubblegum toothpaste and mouthwash over potential contamination with outside hormones, according to an FDA warning letter to Signature Formulations issued Jan. 21, 2026.
 That letter said the company made products on shared equipment and that its cleaning process was not adequately validated to prevent cross-contamination. Equipment used for another product was used before making the kids' toothpaste, the FDA said. The agency also cited repeat problems from a 2018 warning letter. In its response, the firm told regulators it does not make drug products, a position the FDA rejected.
 The FDA redacted the name of the ingredient involved but warned that in children, exposure to even low levels "can lead to developmental and reproductive harm." The agency asked the manufacturer to test all of its drug products for the contaminant and to test retained samples of batches still on the market.
 MedShadow reported that Signature Formulations manufactures ORL products and also makes supplements that include bioidentical progesterone and estrogen. The current recall names ORL Labs as the recalling firm.
 Health Concerns for Children and Adults
 A Class II recall means the products may cause temporary or medically reversible health effects, and the chance of serious harm is considered remote. Toothpaste and mouthwash are meant to be spit out, though young children often swallow some toothpaste, which is one reason children's products draw extra concern. The amount of hormone exposure from these products is unknown.
 Children are generally more sensitive to outside hormones than adults. In 2010, the FDA warned that young children accidentally exposed to an estradiol spray through skin contact with adult users developed signs of early puberty, including breast development, HealthDay reported . That case involved a different product and route of exposure, and no similar effects have been linked to ORL products.
 Key questions remain open. The FDA has not said which products contained which hormone, how much was found or how long contaminated lots were on sale. With expiration dates running into 2028, some recalled tubes and bottles may stay in homes for a long time.
 DHEA is an adrenal hormone sold in supplements, and the body can convert it into testosterone and estrogen. Adults with hormone-sensitive conditions, such as some breast cancers, or who are pregnant may want to mention any use of the recalled products to their clinician.
 Steps for Households With Recalled Products
 People who have any of the six products should stop using them. Check the UPC on the box or tube and the lot number printed on the package. Recalled items can be thrown away or returned to the retailer to ask about a refund. Online listings may not all have been removed, so the lot number matters more than where a product was bought.
 Health officials have not recommended routine testing for children who used the products. Parents can call a pediatrician if a child shows signs such as breast development, pubic hair or a sudden growth spurt at an unusually young age, or unexplained vaginal bleeding in a young girl. Bring the product packaging to the appointment if possible.
 Shoppers who bought ORL products online can check past orders for product names and dates before searching their bathroom shelves. Side effects can be reported to the FDA's MedWatch program at 1-800-FDA-1088. MedicalDaily will report any update to the recall or any new FDA findings on hormone levels.

 Key Questions Answered
 Which products are recalled? Six ORL Organic Oral Care items: three 4-ounce toothpastes and three 16.9-ounce mouthwashes, including kids' versions.
 Why were they recalled? FDA testing found progesterone, estradiol or DHEA in samples. The company attributed this to cross-contamination.
 How many units are affected? About 51,762 units sold nationwide.
 Has anyone gotten sick? No illnesses have been reported.
 How serious is a Class II recall? The FDA says Class II products may cause temporary or reversible health effects, and serious harm is remote.
 What should I do with recalled products? Stop using them, check the UPC and lot number, then discard them or contact the retailer.
 When should a child see a doctor? If a child shows signs of early puberty, such as breast development or pubic hair at a young age, call a pediatrician.
